a70.speaker: Paulus Noa, Director General of Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission
a70.speech: "I must point out that it is not required that all corruption cases must be dealt with through criminal courts, because not all corrupt conduct meets criminal elements that merit criminal prosecution." ; "Charge the culprits with misconduct charges, and if found guilty, deal with them appropriately. Do not depend on prosecution for every corrupt act. Prosecution has its own various causes of delays."

a70.speaker: Paulus Noa, Director General of Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission
a70.speech: "This is particularly significant. It highlights the vital role the youth can play in shaping a future where integrity is championed, and corruption is not tolerated. Youth is an invaluable asset to any nation. They are game-changers." ; Said young people, being at the prime of their lives, embody many positive qualities, and that Namibia must recognise the role of youth in raising anti-corruption awareness and building a stronger good governance system. ; "This is more particularly the case given the fact that in Namibia, youth represent much of the population, at 70%, according to the Namibia Statistics Agency's recent national census. This fact calls for active participation of youth in national developmental programmes, including good governance."

a70.speaker: Paulus Noa, Director General of Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission
a70.speech: Said the commission is ready to work with the communities the new Rundu office will serve. ; "The office belongs to the public, and we expect the public to make use of the office to the fullest. Raise anti-corruption awareness by engaging the officials in the office, reporting allegations of corruption to the office, and providing constructive suggestions and opinions on the best ways of preventing corruption to the office. Support the officials to succeed in their efforts. Where you observe that they demonstrate a lack of commitment or conduct themselves in an undesirable manner, raise your concerns to the relevant authorities."

a70.speaker: Bonifatius Wakudumo, Kavango East Governor
a70.speech: Stated that corruption is a global phenomenon that hinders development and fosters inequality. "It poses a direct threat to poverty reduction and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals." ; "In Namibia, citizens have united to express strong rejection of corruption and to demand that the government takes more drastic action to combat this threat and ensure unity, democracy, and the promotion of equitable development for all. This call for action must be acknowledged by all. Every Namibian has a role to play in the fight against corruption, and it is important for everyone to contribute and be part of the fight against corruption."

a165.speaker: Dr Gaoussou Karamoko, Director General of the DGIE (Directorate-General for Ivorians Abroad)
a165.speech: Set out several key points to be addressed at the workshop in his opening remarks, saying the reintegration of migrants is a reality linking Côte d'Ivoire to Europe, a global issue, and that migrants form a link connecting the two regions, while stressing that "now, it is up to Côte d'Ivoire to fully complete this reintegration process."

a165.speaker: Anne-Catherine Claude, representative of the European Union
a165.speech: "The MPRR project is being revised to add additional financial resources which it currently lacks."

a165.speaker: David Preux, Head of Mission of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Côte d'Ivoire
a165.speech: Stressed the need for a coordinated approach through a national consultation framework, noting that such an initiative would help strengthen efforts to further structure support for returning migrants.

a217.speaker: United States (government pledge)
a217.speech: Pledges 150 million dollars in support to Ethiopia's health sector a year to fight tuberculosis; HIV/AIDS; malaria; maternal, neonatal and child health; nutrition; and water, sanitation and hygiene.

a407.speaker: Competition and Tariff Commission (CTC), Zimbabwe
a407.speech: Says the pending agreement on tariff modalities for critical sectors like textiles and clothing, fish and motor vehicles by member countries on the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), is delaying operationalisation of the new platform.

a423.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
a423.speech: Said the association, beginning from Sene 30, 2017 (Ethiopian calendar), has designated the rainy season (kiremt) as "Reading Day" and is working to develop the reading culture within society ; "Kiremt is when schools close. At this time it is necessary to make sure children do not spend their time in inappropriate places," explaining that the association's general assembly decided to make Sene 30 Reading Day so that children spend their time in reading, in knowledge and in enjoyment.

a423.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
a423.speech: Said that if a reading revolution is to come to Ethiopia the work must not be left to the Ethiopian Writers' Association alone, that at present the writer, the journalist, the politician, the religious father and other sections of society are not seen reading, and that almost everyone has turned his back on reading.

a423.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
a423.speech: "At present, with the spread of social media, most people spend the day glued to their mobile phones," adding that the parent therefore stays away from reading and the child, seeing this, also drifts away, and that if the parent does not explain the benefit of reading and cannot be a role model, the present and future generations will be a cause for concern ; "A parent who wants to lead children onto a good path, and a teacher who strives for a good student to emerge, must first read themselves if they want to have a reading child and student," since children imitate what they see.

a423.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
a423.speech: Said the Ministry of Education, being the ministry of knowledge, should take the lead in making reading a habit among children, that the Ministry of Culture and Sport is also expected to give attention to this, and that every well-intentioned Ethiopian who cares about tomorrow's generation should care about children's reading culture.

a423.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
a423.speech: Stated that the mass media bear great responsibility for growing children's reading culture, and that just as every European footballer's shoe size and the number of rooms in his house are broadcast on FM radio stations until European football seems Ethiopian, the same amount of work should be done to make reading a culture among Ethiopians.

a423.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
a423.speech: Said she has produced two children's books titled "Adey Sitnesa" and "Amoditna Gomaditna," and that the books have been distributed in schools and bookshops.

a423.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
a423.speech: "For children's reading culture to develop, the homework has first to be done at the level of the family. Because children accept and follow what they see, the family has a responsibility for the growth of children's reading habit," adding that even parents whose children have not yet reached reading age should have the habit of reading books to them, that parents should set aside a time of day even out of tight schedules, and that since children are becoming victims of technology the family must work hard so that children turn away from the phone and towards reading.

a423.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
a423.speech: "One cannot say a child is reading merely because he spent the day at school. Parents are expected to make their children work hard at reading today in order to see their child's bright and good tomorrow," expressing her belief that if books were made available at public gatherings, walks, bazaars and exhibitions — as tents are pitched and trading takes place during religious and public holidays — and if reading were preached there, the reading culture in Ethiopia would grow again.

a423.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
a423.speech: Explained that her ten-year-old child has so far read 245 books ; "I make my child read children's books and selected adult books," recalling that there had been a campaign at the German Cultural Centre called "When Ethiopia Reads, Germany Helps," that the writer and translator Yonas Tarekegn made great efforts to grow children's reading culture by inviting authors to schools and donating books, that she herself took part in this work, and that it contributed to the development of her child's reading culture.

a423.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
a423.speech: Said that if children are to become readers the parent must be a reader; that studies indicate parents should read books to children up to the age of ten, and that applying this to her own child made him successful ; "We should not have children read adult or children's books before we ourselves have read them first," explaining that during the coronavirus pandemic, when schools closed and children's books could not be found, she let her child read selected adult books, but only those she believed would add to his knowledge and assist his development.

a423.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
a423.speech: Explained that her child's habitual reading has made him successful in his academic studies, bold enough to ask about what he does not understand, and able to carry out tasks in a reasoned and accountable manner ; "When we gather at home and watch the news, we allow ideas to circulate. Although the news of the present time is full of war, the practice of watching is long-standing within the family," saying the discussions made her realise her child grieves at the crisis war brings and is an ardent seeker of peace, and that the substantial thoughts he raises about the war between Palestine and Israel come from reading books.

a423.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
a423.speech: Said children are a reflection of what they see, that parents should allocate time and develop the habit of reading with their children, and that because children resemble their family, parents are expected to be role models by reading books.

a423.speaker: Studies (cited)
a423.speech: Studies indicate that parents should read books to children up to the age of ten.

a596.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a596.speech: Says suspension of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) programmes globally by the Trump administration is long overdue and a wake-up call for African countries to grow their economies by enhancing bilateral trade and investment among themselves; says the development also calls for prudent management of resources; notes that socio-economic growth can only be attained with increased investment, trade and transaction among African countries; welcomed United States President Donald Trump's order to freeze funding to all UNAIDS programmes: "It is long overdue, it is actually long overdue because it underscores the importance of us on the continent growing our economies, focusing on growth, growth and more growth."

a596.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a596.speech: Has called for the closure of USAID citing unprecedented levels of corruption.

a596.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS executive director and UN under-secretary general
a596.speech: Said there is now need to free domestic resources for investing in health.

a596.speaker: Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation (news item)
a596.speech: Cited as the source of the report: "This is according to a news item monitored on the Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation last evening."

a684.speaker: Joël Kouadio N'Guessan, Ivorian politician and former minister (statement from detention)
a684.speech: Presented his apologies to the judicial institution and to Ivorian magistrates, expressing his regrets following an interview granted to the online newspaper Lemondeactuel.com on 17 June; acknowledged that his remarks had shocked several actors in the judicial system: "Far be it from me to call into question the authority of the judicial institution or to damage the honour of Ivorian magistrates," he declared, before offering his "sincere apologies" to the magistrates and to the judicial institution as a whole.

a827.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti and current Chairman of IGAD, and Lawrence Korbani, IGAD Special Envoy to Sudan
a827.speech: Their discussions highlighted the perfect convergence of views of the two parties on the need to give priority, in IGAD’s mediation in Sudan, to the establishment of a ceasefire and to the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid in that country, these being the immediate objectives the regional organisation assigns to its agenda in Sudan, ahead of influencing the warring parties towards a political settlement of the Sudanese crisis in a second phase.

a852.speaker: Bank of Namibia (BoN), latest Annual Report
a852.speech: "Much in line with the national slogan, “Land of the Brave,” the MFPE, the Bank, and its participant partners did not shy away from adversity and less-than-desired outcomes" ; "Instead, they regrouped, retried and ultimately helped to improve the lives of Namibians who are both directly and indirectly associated with the SMEs that have benefited from the SME Economic Recovery Scheme."

a852.speaker: Bank of Namibia (BoN)
a852.speech: According to the BoN, the success of the SME Economic Recovery Loan Scheme stands as a testament to the resilience and collaborative spirit ingrained within Namibia's ethos.

a881.speaker: Liberia Revenue Authority / Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (press release)
a881.speech: Said the crucial meeting underscored the importance of deepened collaboration between the two government entities in mobilizing and efficiently collecting revenue to support Liberia’s development agenda; both parties reaffirmed their commitment to working together more effectively to address challenges and capitalize on opportunities for revenue growth through the full implementation of the country’s revenue laws.

a881.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a881.speech: “We have come to receive an update on revenue performance and gain deeper insights into the challenges you face. Our goal is to work collaboratively to enhance revenue generation and drive national development.”

a881.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a881.speech: Commended the LRA for exceeding its 2024 revenue target, and expressed optimism for sustained growth and stronger fiscal management in the years ahead.

a881.speaker: James Dorbor Jallah, Commissioner General of the Liberia Revenue Authority
a881.speech: Acknowledged the Ministry’s continued support, which he credited as a key factor in the LRA’s success; he outlined a couple of challenges and emphasized the need for increased budgetary allocation to address them and to enable the Authority to meet its ambitious domestic revenue target of US$804.6 million for 2025.

a901.speaker: Global Water Partnership Organisation (statement on the GWPO website)
a901.speech: “GWP faces an evolving international context, with shifting foreign aid priorities and increasing engagement from emerging economies. Alex will steer the organisation and improve the necessary governance protocols to embrace this new reality, exploring fresh partnerships and funding opportunities with nations and institutions that share GWP’s vision of a water secure world” ; according to the statement, Alex will lead the establishment of GWPO regional hubs that, together with GWP Regional Water Partnerships, will serve as engines of a bold transformative agenda on integrated investments in water security and climate resilience ; “This shift aims to better serve our regions and also bring us closer to our country partners facing increased water risks and challenges” ; “He has a proven track record of working with Heads of States, global and business leaders, in mobilising investments at scale. He pioneered the establishment of the first-ever International High-Level Panel on Water Investments for Africa, comprising 20 sitting and former Heads of State, and global leaders. Alex spearheaded support to the African Union (AU) in the development of the Continental Africa Water Investment Programme (AIP), which the Panel supports in its aim to close the water investment gap in Africa by mobilising $30 billion annually by 2030.”

a901.speaker: Ban Ki-Moon, 8th UN Secretary-General
a901.speech: Commended the AIP’s transformative approach and called on global leaders and international organisations to scale up the AIP globally.

a901.speaker: Pablo Bereciartua, Chair of GWP’s Steering Committee
a901.speech: “We are pleased to have Alex lead GWP during this dynamic phase full of opportunities. His ability to build partnerships, mobilise resources, and lead diverse teams makes him the ideal person to drive GWP’s vision and mission of water security for all. As GWP strengthens its network, develops new ways to grow its resources, and increases its regional impact, we are confident that Alex’s leadership will amplify our global reach.”

a901.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a901.speech: Named the AIP as one of the key game-changing initiatives and commitments of the UN Water Action Agenda, aimed at driving transformation from a global water crisis to a water-secure world.

a901.speaker: Jakaya Kikwete, Former President of the United Republic of Tanzania and Chair of the Board for GWP Southern Africa
a901.speech: Welcomed the GWP Steering Committee decision as ‘a wise decision’, and applauded his leadership abilities stating that: “Mr Simalabwi has been an exemplary GWPSA Executive Secretary and CEO – a visionary, diligent, and hands-on leader whose contributions have significantly advanced GWPSA’s mission”.

a901.speaker: Alex Simalabwi, incoming GWP Executive Secretary and CEO
a901.speech: “I am honoured to take on this role at such a pivotal time. For over two decades, GWP has been at the forefront of integrated water resources management. Now is the right time to change the status quo – pushed by the new global political dynamics and opening of new opportunities – and build on this strong foundation of GWP for bigger and stronger impacts, with unprecedented acceleration in both the pace and scale of mobilisation of climate-resilient water investments, in response to the current global water and climate emergency. I welcome the opportunity to join hands with global leaders and partners to lead the step-change of GWP into a transformative partner of choice for climate-resilient water investments. In the words of Nelson Mandela, ‘it always seems impossible until it is done.’”

a1111.speaker: John Travolta, actor and Grease co-star
a1111.speech: Said she "made all of our lives so much better" ; wrote on Instagram: "Your impact was incredible. I love you so much. We will see you down the road and we will all be together again." "Yours from the first moment I saw you and forever!" he added, signing off: "Your Danny, your John!"

a1111.speaker: Randal Kleiser, director of Grease
a1111.speech: Said: "What you see is what you get with her." ; said he had been friends with Newton-John for 40 years and "she never changed, she was always exactly the way everyone imagines her". "She was charming, lovely, warm… There are so many clichés you can say about her but in her case it was all true." Asked what his everlasting memory of her will be, he told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Hanging out with her at her ranch. Seeing the real Olivia which was exactly like the Olivia she projected. No cameras around, no people around… she was exactly the same and as loving as ever."

a1111.speaker: Stockard Channing, actress who played Rizzo in Grease
a1111.speech: Said: "I don't know if I've known a lovelier human being. Olivia was the essence of summer – her sunniness, her warmth and her grace are what always come to mind when I think of her. I will miss her enormously."

a1111.speaker: Rod Stewart, singer
a1111.speech: Called her "the perfect lady, gorgeous, with great poise and with a certain Aussie sophistication". "Her spandex trousers in Grease were my inspiration for my 'Da ya think I'm Sexy' era," he added.

a1111.speaker: Oprah Winfrey, US television host
a1111.speech: Said her "positivity was just infectious". "You'll be missed, Olivia," she wrote. "Here's to the good times."

a1111.speaker: Dionne Warwick, singer
a1111.speech: Called Newton-John "one of the nicest people I had the pleasure of recording and performing with".

a1111.speaker: Hospital that runs the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Wellness and Research Centre in Melbourne (statement)
a1111.speech: In a statement, said she "encouraged, inspired and supported" staff and patients everyday. "We are incredibly grateful for the special relationship we had with Olivia for many years. Her generous support and gift provided hope and changed the lives of thousands of cancer patients… She was the light at the end of the tunnel for many, many people."

a1111.speaker: John Easterling, Olivia Newton-John's husband (statement on social media)
a1111.speech: Said she had died on Monday as he hailed her as "a symbol of triumphs and hope for over 30 years sharing her journey with breast cancer". "Her healing inspiration and pioneering experience with plant medicine continues with the Olivia Newton-John Foundation Fund, dedicated to researching plant medicine and cancer."

a1111.speaker: Olivia Newton-John, singer and actress
a1111.speech: "It annoys me when people think because it's commercial, it's bad," she told Rolling Stone. "It's completely opposite. If people like it, that's what it's supposed to be."

a1111.speaker: Olivia Newton-John, singer and actress
a1111.speech: In 2019, after being diagnosed with breast cancer for the third time, she was asked by CBS News how she coped: "It was consuming my day and after a time I went 'you know what', I need to enjoy my life so I'm going to eat a cookie if I want it." "Because the joy of life and everyday living has to be a part of that healing process as well. So I've chosen that path to be grateful and to feel good about things because the other side's not so good."

a1133.speaker: Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, President of Somalia's Southwest State
a1133.speech: Speaking at the signing ceremony, stressed the law's significance and reaffirmed his administration's commitment to its implementation: "I am very pleased to enact this law to ensure humanitarian aid is distributed fairly to those who need it most. I extend my gratitude to everyone involved in making this possible, and the law will take effect immediately."

a1133.speaker: Humanitarian experts and NGOs
a1133.speech: Welcomed the move, expressing optimism that the legislation will improve the efficiency of aid operations in a region where drought, displacement, and food insecurity remain pressing issues.

a1168.speaker: Government of Cabo Verde (Facebook post)
a1168.speech: According to the government's Facebook post, the prime minister was in S. Miguel and met "with farmers to assess the impacts of this water mobilisation policy"; it was reported that drip irrigation has produced concrete results, guaranteeing water availability, and that the government contributes 50% of the cost of the materials.

a1318.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), in collaboration with the Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE) and other partners
a1318.speech: Has urged the media to prioritise child rights and protection reports and to elevate the issues of child rights and protection to the forefront of public discourse, in order to enhance the lives of Nigeria's 110 million children.

a1318.speaker: Stakeholders at the symposium
a1318.speech: Stressed the critical role of the media in advocating for the well-being and rights of children across the nation.

a1318.speaker: UNICEF report, "The State of Nigeria's Children: Summary of the 2024 Situational Analysis of Children and Adolescents in Nigeria"
a1318.speech: Showed disturbing statistics that nearly half of all Nigerian children live in poverty, 41 out of every 1,000 newborns die before their first birthday, and 2.1 million children remain unvaccinated ; also revealed that 4.9 million children are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, that 40 percent of children under five are stunted due to malnutrition, and that eight percent suffer from wasting.

a1318.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF's representative in Nigeria
a1318.speech: Stressed the transformative power of the media in influencing policy, public perception, and urgent action to improve children's lives. "Media can drive change by keeping children's issues at the top of the national agenda." ; Argued that the media must move beyond reporting daily events to deliberate, sustained advocacy that holds stakeholders accountable ; "This includes the federal and state governments, religious and traditional leaders, and families. You are uniquely positioned to inform and equip these stakeholders with the tools to protect children's rights." ; "Childhood is short - just 18 years. The changes we make today are the only ones that matter to these children. The media has the power to create a sense of urgency and push for the immediate actions that children cannot wait for."

a1318.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF's representative in Nigeria
a1318.speech: Noted that nearly half of Nigerian children live in poverty, with 67 percent experiencing multidimensional deprivations such as malnutrition, lack of education, and inadequate healthcare; additionally, 2.1 million children remain unvaccinated, 4.9 million need urgent humanitarian aid, and three out of four children in school are failing to meet basic literacy and numeracy standards.

a1318.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF's representative in Nigeria
a1318.speech: Cited past examples where media pressure influenced government action, such as stepping in to protect children from harsh judicial punishments ; challenged media organisations to celebrate progress and positive developments for children while maintaining a focus on the urgent need for reforms in education, healthcare, and poverty alleviation ; encouraged media to foster competition among states in achieving milestones like open defecation-free status and improving access to food and education, affirming that by amplifying solutions and inspiring collaboration, the media can change the narrative for Nigeria's children and help secure their future.

a1318.speaker: Eze Anaba, President of the Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE)
a1318.speech: Urged media practitioners to take a more proactive role in advocating for the rights and well-being of Nigerian children, underscoring the urgent need to address pressing issues affecting children, including malnutrition, lack of education, and vulnerability to preventable diseases. "Children in Nigeria are still dying from diseases that have been eradicated elsewhere or for which vaccinations are available. This situation demands a collective effort from media practitioners, health workers, policymakers, and the government to declare a state of emergency for children and place them at the forefront of national priorities." ; Highlighted the stark realities facing children in Nigeria, where nearly half of the 220 million population are underage, adding that millions of children are out of school, subjected to abuse, child labor, and early marriages, while others face violence and recruitment as child combatants in conflict-affected regions ; "These statistics are not just numbers; they are stories of children whose rights are being denied and whose dreams are deferred."

a1318.speaker: Eze Anaba, President of the Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE)
a1318.speech: Noted that the symposium brought together senior government officials, media practitioners, advocates, and stakeholders, united in their commitment to creating a society where every child can thrive ; enjoined journalists and editors to wield their storytelling power to inspire and drive societal change. "The media is not just a passive observer of society but an active participant in shaping norms and influencing policies. We must uncover and amplify the voices of the voiceless and pressure policymakers to act." ; Emphasized the need for solution-based journalism that highlights problems while exploring and advocating for remedies, and stressed the importance of celebrating progress alongside addressing challenges ; "Partnerships with organisations like UNICEF can provide data and tools to strengthen advocacy. We must commit to actionable steps, whether through investigative reports, collaborations with NGOs, or dedicated platforms for child rights." ; Citing Nelson Mandela, said, "There can be no keener revelation of a society's soul than the way it treats its children," and challenged the media to become the conscience of society.

a1318.speaker: Tunde Onakoya, founder of Chess in Slums Africa
a1318.speech: Stated in his presentation on the 'urgency of the situation' that nearly half of seven million Nigerian children live in abject poverty, with Nigeria being one of the countries with the youngest population in the world ; warned that if deliberate measures are not taken to invest in the capacity of Nigerian children, they will have no part to play in the world's future ; "The real Nigerian challenge is the struggle of the Nigerian child. Nigeria will be the world's future workforce in the next 50 years, like Europe. If we have 20 million children out of school who do not have any skills or education, how will they participate in that future? There really would be no place for them in the world if they don't have the education to contribute meaningfully to global markets. So what happens is that they will become liabilities in the future because they have no value to give. The world wants assets, and it desires an educated workforce to come and build economies."

a1323.speaker: International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Ghana
a1323.speech: Has eulogised Alhaji Asoma Banda, saying his life's work remains a beacon for future generations of entrepreneurs and leaders ; reaffirms its commitment to the principles he so passionately upheld - free and fair trade, business integrity and sustainable development.

a1323.speaker: Emmanuel Doni Kwame, Secretary General of ICC Ghana (tribute statement)
a1323.speech: The tribute recounted some of the achievements of the business mogul, who touched many lives in Ghana and abroad. "Sadly, we had to succumb to the implications of the news of the last voyage on earth of the transport mogul that Alhaji Asoma Abu Banda, our founder and prime mover, was." ; "In the run-up to Ghana's independence, Alhaji was known to have taken on the gruelling task of buying cattle from the Sahel provinces of our sub-region and transporting them to Kumasi. This underscored for him, firsthand, the undeniable need to adopt cooperation as a key factor in promoting international commerce, even during those days." ; "A fully-fledged pioneering force in international shipping, land transport and aviation, Alhaji Banda exemplified fortitude, the very principles upon which the ICC International was founded, namely promoting trade, fostering economic growth and advancing global prosperity." ; Said Alhaji Asoma Abu Banda fell "with the abiding faith that the guiding spirit he represented and the footsteps he was leaving on the sands of time would serve as a trusted mariner's chart for all those who might travel without the fear of losing their way on the uncharted waters, land and airways of modern international trade."

a1381.speaker: Dr Natu ElMaamry Mwamba, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance of Tanzania
a1381.speech: Speaking at the launch in Dodoma, said that the Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) was developed to improve revenue collection, enhance policy predictability and boost public confidence; the strategy focuses on closing loopholes and reducing fiscal deficits to achieve a more sustainable and equitable tax framework, she said, and it is aimed at reducing the nation's reliance on foreign aid and commercial loans. She said the approach was developed through collaboration with development partners and the private sector, and noted that it outlines key reforms across three main areas: tax policy, revenue administration and legal frameworks.

a1381.speaker: Dr Natu ElMaamry Mwamba, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance of Tanzania
a1381.speech: Said the MTRS has taken into account national economic trends and risks and incorporating mitigation strategies to ensure smooth implementation; she pointed out that similar frameworks have been successfully applied in other African countries, including Kenya, Uganda, Malawi, Sierra Leone, Ghana, Morocco and Rwanda.

a1381.speaker: Johnson Nyella, Commissioner of the Policy Analysis Department
a1381.speech: According to him, the strategy was prepared with technical support from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and is a foundational step towards building a strong, self-reliant economy. "This is about ensuring our country has the capacity to generate sufficient domestic resources to finance its own budget, foster selfreliance and achieve sustainable and resilient development."

a1419.speaker: Convergence, the global network for blended finance
a1419.speech: According to Convergence, agriculture, energy and financial services account for the largest share of blended finance transactions (>70%) to date, making the country's priorities especially well aligned with the existing blended finance market.

a1419.speaker: Ethiopian Government's Ten Year (2021-2030) Development Plan, 'A Pathway to Prosperity'
a1419.speech: Prioritizes agriculture, energy and financial services as a means to double per capita income by 2030.

a1419.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a1419.speech: The Government of Ethiopia would like to assess the potential of blended finance in terms of financing its development agenda.

a1489.speaker: Hamas (statement)
a1489.speech: Has reaffirmed that it will not agree to disarm unless a sovereign Palestinian state is established, in response to one of Israel’s key demands in talks about a ceasefire in Gaza. Hamas said in its statement that it could not yield its right to “resistance and its weapons” unless an “independent, fully sovereign Palestinian state with Jerusalem as its capital” was established.

a1489.speaker: Steve Witkoff, US President Donald Trump’s Middle East envoy
a1489.speech: Hamas said it was responding to remarks it attributed to Witkoff that Hamas had “expressed its willingness” to lay down its weapons.

a1489.speaker: Steve Witkoff, US President Donald Trump’s Middle East envoy
a1489.speech: Said peace efforts should focus on ending the conflict and bringing home all the hostages, instead of what he called a partial deal.

a1489.speaker: Arab governments
a1489.speech: In the past few days, Arab governments have urged Hamas to disarm and surrender control of Gaza.

a1489.speaker: United Kingdom government
a1489.speech: The UK said it would recognise a state of Palestine if Israel did not meet certain conditions by September.

a1489.speaker: Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, Israel Defense Forces
a1489.speech: Warned on Friday that there would be no respite in fighting in Gaza if negotiations failed to quickly secure the release of hostages being held by Hamas.

a1489.speaker: Family of hostage Evyatar David (statement)
a1489.speech: Issued a statement after Hamas released a video showing him shirtless and emaciated in a dimly-lit tunnel. They accused Hamas of starving him as part of a propaganda campaign and appealed to the Israeli government and the United States to do everything possible to save him.

a1489.speaker: UN agencies
a1489.speech: Have warned there is man-made, mass starvation in Gaza, and have blamed Israel, which controls the entry of all supplies to the territory.

a1489.speaker: Israeli government
a1489.speech: Israel has insisted there are no restrictions on aid deliveries and that there is “no starvation”.

a1489.speaker: United Nations
a1489.speech: Latest figures from the United Nations say at least 1,373 Palestinians have been killed seeking food since late May. The majority have been killed by the Israeli military near Israeli and US-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) distribution sites, the UN says.

a1489.speaker: Israeli military
a1489.speech: Israel has accused Hamas of instigating chaos near the sites and says its troops do not intentionally open fire on civilians.

a1489.speaker: Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry
a1489.speech: According to the territory’s Hamas-run health ministry, more than 60,000 people have been killed in Gaza, and 169 people, including 93 children, have died from malnutrition.

a1526.speaker: Lookman, young Beninese street vendor of steering-wheel covers and windscreen shades
a1526.speech: Recounts in a calm tone, with a pang in his heart, how the reckless driver who tore off the shred of flesh from his finger did not even bother to stop and show sympathy for his pain: "I was bleeding heavily so I went to the hospital to get it dressed. It's true it still hurts... but it will pass."

a1526.speaker: Ramatou Koné, street vendor of cigarettes and tissues
a1526.speech: Adds: "What are we going to do? We are between life and death," before setting off in pursuit of her customers.

a1526.speaker: Street traders (collectively)
a1526.speech: Have nicknamed the officers of the brigade against urban disorder "Bacongo's men" and describe them as their bête noire.

a1526.speaker: Autonomous District of Abidjan / Ibrahima Cissé Bacongo, Minister-Governor (official decision)
a1526.speech: Banned, in April 2024, within the district's territory, street vending on major thoroughfares (avenues, highways, boulevards, roads connecting the municipalities), begging in all its forms and in all places, the use of handcarts (Wottro), and the production, importation, distribution, marketing and use of plastic bags, with the stated aim of cleaning up the population's living environment, further ensuring the safety of persons and property, and improving traffic flow.

a1526.speaker: Grâce, 11-year-old schoolgirl selling sachets of water
a1526.speech: "I've been here since 7 o'clock. I'm on my third packet of water. On each packet I make a profit of 1,500 CFA francs. But I only sell when I don't have classes" ; on the subject of checks by "Bacongo's people": "Those people don't just take away the goods. When they catch you, they send you to prison."

a1526.speaker: Fréjuste Koffi, street vendor of water sachets, Boulevard Latrille, Deux-Plateaux
a1526.speech: Recounts his ordeal: "It was in February, the day after Valentine's Day, that Bacongo's people caught us. There were many of us. Among us were women and even minors. They first took us to the sub-prefecture, from there we went to Plateau. After the trial, they took us straight to the Maca. I did two weeks there. I even fell ill. In any case, a normal man who ends up there necessarily falls ill. But since I hadn't stolen anything, they released me. I didn't pay anything. But since the State has said it's forbidden, they just wanted to frighten us."

a1526.speaker: Fréjuste Koffi, street vendor of water sachets, Boulevard Latrille, Deux-Plateaux
a1526.speech: Asked why he continues the activity despite this, replies: "What am I going to do? Rest brings hardship (lack of money). It's from this activity that I live" ; confides that he has new techniques: "If you don't know anyone here and you're not familiar with the people who own the shops, they'll certainly catch you quickly. Since the shop owners know us, when we see them we go inside their shops. But for the past two days it has become even more complicated, because in addition to 'Bacongo's people', the town hall's officers are also hunting us. Worse, they're in plain clothes. With both groups, no negotiation is possible. They can show up at any moment. There's even a sweet-bread seller who has been at the Maca since April. Apparently they still haven't released her." For Fréjuste, street vending is meant for courageous people.

a1526.speaker: Marie-Jeanne, young seller of plantain chips
a1526.speech: Stresses: "If you don't know how to run, you can't sell here. If you don't know where the hiding places are, you can't sell here. We risk our lives here to have something to survive on."

a1526.speaker: Mamadou Bagayoko, handcart (wottro) operator based at a garage in Abobo Anador
a1526.speech: Having arrived in Côte d'Ivoire two months ago, he says he carries out this activity without worry.

a1526.speaker: Ivorian law of 2013 banning certain street activities (Article 21)
a1526.speech: Provides that any violation of the provisions of the aforementioned Article 19 is punishable by imprisonment of 2 to 6 months and a fine of 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs, or one of these two penalties; in the event of a repeat offence, the fine is doubled.

a1553.speaker: Ivaldo Quincardete, provincial director of Education of Cabo Delgado
a1553.speech: "The work has really come to a standstill. It is about 60 to 65% complete. And we are waiting for an official announcement" ; assured that "If USAID really does not continue, there are partners in good faith who are willing to complete the work."

a1574.speaker: Admassu Tadesse, Group President and Managing Director of Trade & Development Bank, and Zainab Ahmed, Executive Director at the World Bank and former Nigerian Minister of Finance (opening keynote speakers)
a1574.speech: Set a powerful tone — challenging participants to move beyond traditional aid models and strengthen Africa's investment readiness.

a1574.speaker: Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, WTO Director-General
a1574.speech: Called for a decisive shift away from reliance on foreign aid, urging African countries to mobilize domestic resources, attract private sector investment, and build institutional trust: "Africa's opportunity lies not in aid — but in adding value, building trust, and using our resources wisely."

a1574.speaker: Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, WTO Director-General
a1574.speech: Stressed that Africa's critical minerals must be leveraged strategically to drive industrialization rather than perpetuate dependence on raw exports: "Our critical minerals are in demand — but instead of giving them away raw, we must negotiate smartly, add value locally, create jobs, and become a true hub of global manufacturing and innovation."

a1574.speaker: Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, WTO Director-General
a1574.speech: Addressed the impacts of global economic shifts — from trade disruptions to shrinking aid budgets — and stressed the urgency of regional collaboration, transparent governance, and strategic investment facilitation to attract both diaspora and global capital.

a1574.speaker: Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, WTO Director-General
a1574.speech: Encouraged African entrepreneurs, leaders, and the diaspora to recognize their individual agency: "Even solving one problem or building one enterprise can have ripple effects across the continent. Everyone has a role to play in building Africa's future."

a1574.speaker: Yvonne Ike, Managing Director and Head of Sub-Saharan Africa (ex-RSA) at Bank of America
a1574.speech: "Events like this roundtable are vital platforms to foster collaboration, deepen trust, and unlock the entrepreneurial potential that exists both within Africa and among its global diaspora. It was an honor to join this important dialogue and help shape conversations that will drive long-term impact."

a1574.speaker: Akaego Okoye, Founder of African Business Stories and Convener of the ABS Roundtable Series
a1574.speech: "Diaspora investment is not just about capital; it's about building ecosystems and reshaping Africa's economic narrative. We are proud to create a platform where action-oriented conversations drive real change."

a1885.speaker: Albertine Houessou, local coordinator of the CBI project
a1885.speech: Presented the results of the evaluation of Cetrab's strategic plan (2022–2024), conducted by Resilience Consultancy in collaboration with CBI and Economic Sense; the evaluation highlighted the progress made while identifying persistent structural challenges, notably the cooperative's financial autonomy.

a1885.speaker: Cyrille Adjahouinou, outgoing president of Cetrab
a1885.speech: Presenting his end-of-term report, recalled the path travelled over the past six years to structure the processed pineapple sector. He praised the collective efforts and the support of technical and financial partners, notably Defia-Enable (today Parsad), Pfd/Pinex and Atda Pôle 7, as well as the new collaboration with the Centre for the Promotion of Imports (CBI) of the Dutch government through its gender-transformative project in the dried pineapple sector in Benin.

a1885.speaker: Muhammadou Awêlou Alidou, incoming president of Cetrab
a1885.speech: Presented his roadmap, centred on resource mobilisation, the professionalisation of member enterprises and strengthening the visibility of the body, which is still too little known nationally and internationally: “We will go looking for partners to support member enterprises, especially the smallest ones, so that they can meet the quality standards required by the markets,” he declared ; Cetrab, according to him, aims in the coming years to become a strong umbrella organisation, representative of all the country's pineapple processors, capable of exporting high-quality products to regional and international markets.

a1997.speaker: Melanie Keita, CEO and co-founder of Melanin Kapital
a1997.speech: spoke about the need for more accessible financing options for Africa’s youth-led startups and questioned whether there were plans to digitise the loan process: “Can people access loans from their living room instead of having to travel a lot of time and then go with a lot of paperwork and being denied loans sometimes?”

a1997.speaker: Maropene Ramokgopa, South Africa’s Minister in the Presidency Responsible for Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation
a1997.speech: told attendees that young African entrepreneurs are “drivers of change” and urged governments to prioritise entrepreneurship policies and reduce bureaucratic barriers: “From financial technology, agriculture, renewable energy and creative sector to digital health solutions, young African entrepreneurs are transforming their communities” ; “They are also creating jobs and reshaping the economies as well.”

a1997.speaker: Ahmed Attout, Director for Financial Sector Development at the African Development Bank
a1997.speech: introduced the Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Banks (YEIB) initiative, designed to de-risk investing in youth entrepreneurs: “[The Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Banks initiative] is a one-stop shop that can give youth access to finance, employment guarantees, employment technical assistance,” adding that the initiative is in the advanced implementation phase in Liberia and Ethiopia.

a1997.speaker: Jules Ngankam, CEO of the African Guarantee Fund
a1997.speech: announced significant progress in delivering solutions for entrepreneurs, saying the Fund has issued $3 billion in guarantees, enabling commercial banks to lend $5 billion to small and medium-sized enterprises.

a1997.speaker: Chiemela Anosike, founder and CEO of Solaris GreenTech
a1997.speech: said the struggle for start-up success is real: “Entrepreneurship is hard. Entrepreneurship in Africa is harder…so, it’s difficult. So, we have programs like this…but then you give us another full-time job because you’re into fundraising and then it’s taking six months. You’re developing just one proposal [for financing] and it’s taking one month plus.”

a1997.speaker: Martha Phiri, African Development Bank Director for Human Capital, Youth and Skills Development
a1997.speech: told the entrepreneurs that the Bank is integrating entrepreneurship skills into its vocational training programs, in recognition that not all graduates will find employment in existing job markets.

a1997.speaker: Tapera Muzira, the African Development Bank’s Lead Expert for Human Capital, Youth and Skills Development
a1997.speech: said the Bank’s Innovation and Entrepreneurship Lab, an online platform that connects African entrepreneurs with resources, financing, and business development services, is closing the information gap that limits youth potential to contribute to economies and communities.

a1997.speaker: Anne Beathe Tvinnereim, Norway’s Minister of International Development
a1997.speech: noted that her country is committed to supporting African youth entrepreneurship, referencing the USAID and Norway-led Financing for Agricultural Small-and-Medium Enterprises in Africa program: “African youth constitute 60% of the population, which is why youth engagement and involvement is central in Norwegian foreign and development policies. Financing entrepreneurs is not enough. We need to build an entrepreneurial culture that supports solid institutional and regulatory frameworks.”

a1997.speaker: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of the African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
a1997.speech: states that the Hamburg Sustainability Conference is organized annually by the United Nations Development Program, the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), the Michael Otto Foundation for Sustainability and the City of Hamburg.

a2028.speaker: Ministry of Health of Malawi
a2028.speech: Has announced three new cases of Mpox in Lilongwe, bringing the number of confirmed cases to 15 since Malawi reported the first in April.

a2028.speaker: Public Health Institute (Malawi)
a2028.speech: "The patients were aged between 17 and 41," the Public Health Institute said recently. "Investigations are underway to establish the possible source of infection and trace contacts."

a2028.speaker: US Department of State
a2028.speech: According to the US Department of State, the US government was pumping more than $350m to Malawi annually.

a2028.speaker: UNAids (Joint UN Programme on HIV and Aids)
a2028.speech: In March this year drew attention to the immediate risks of the US funding cuts on HIV programmes in the country.

a2028.speaker: Malawian healthcare authorities
a2028.speech: Say drug shortages have forced some patients to stop taking HIV medication.

a2028.speaker: Richard Mvula, Lilongwe District Health Office spokesperson
a2028.speech: "A commonality about these cases is that some were immunocompromised."

a2028.speaker: Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)
a2028.speech: Reports 52,082 cases since January, with over 1,770 deaths during the outbreak as a whole.

a2028.speaker: Africa CDC officials
a2028.speech: Told journalists last week that they were seeing different patterns of transmission between countries and that the continent would need about 6.4 million doses of vaccine, but had only 1.3 million so far; they also highlighted a lack of testing capacity in many countries and warned that in Sierra Leone, where the virus was spreading "exponentialy", patients were being treated two to a bed.

a2028.speaker: Steven Banda, taxi driver
a2028.speech: "I came across a Ministry of Health official who advised that we should be careful since it is dangerous. She described the symptoms, including swellings and mentioned some of the districts affected. I'm not aware of any cases in my area or seen anyone suffering from the disease. We don't know much about it."

a2028.speaker: Dr Victor Mithi, Society of Medical Doctors president
a2028.speech: Said there is need for significant vigilance among practitioners within hospitals to ensure that "as we perform our day-to-day clinical procedures, we are able to screen those patients that may be having this condition" ; "It is a big concern because in Malawi, most people live in crowded houses and still believe that as a form of expression of love, you need to shake hands, you need to hug people and all those things which are basically the risk factors in the transmission of this disease." ; said that with the lessons from Covid-19 and other infectious diseases, Malawi had the capacity to manage mpox, at clinical and community level.

a2028.speaker: Dr Victor Mithi, Society of Medical Doctors president
a2028.speech: "The challenge exists though because of the withdrawal of the US aid. The capacity of our healthcare system is no longer the same." ; According to the doctor, donors contribute almost 60 percent of Malawi's healthcare spending—and over half of the donor aid was coming from the US. ; "Our healthcare system is completely shaken. We are left in a state where we didn't build internal capacities to sustain ourselves."

a2042.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2042.speech: Has said he will cut all future funding to South Africa over allegations that it was confiscating land and "treating certain classes of people very badly" ; wrote on his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday: "I will be cutting off all future funding to South Africa until a full investigation of this situation has been completed!" ; later said, in a briefing with journalists, that South Africa's "leadership is doing some terrible things, horrible things" ; "So that's under investigation right now. We'll make a determination, and until such time as we find out what South Africa is doing — they're taking away land and confiscating land, and actually they're doing things that are perhaps far worse than that."

a2042.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a2042.speech: Responded in a statement on X on Monday morning: "South Africa is a constitutional democracy that is deeply rooted in the rule of law, justice and equality. The South African government has not confiscated any land."

a2042.speaker: Elon Musk, Trump adviser
a2042.speech: Said to Ramaphosa in a post on X: "Why do you have openly racist ownership laws?"

a2042.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South Africa's International Relations Minister
a2042.speech: Said in a response on X that he hoped Trump's advisers would use "this investigative period to deepen their understanding of South Africa's policies as a constitutional democracy" ; "Such insights will ensure a respectful and informed approach to our democratic commitments."

a2042.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a2042.speech: Said in his response that the new law was not a "confiscation instrument, but a constitutionally mandated legal process that ensures public access to land in an equitable and just manner as guided by the constitution" ; said there was no other funding that is received by South Africa from the US except for the US health initiative Pepfar, which he said represented "17% of South Africa's HIV/Aids programme".

a2042.speaker: US government data
a2042.speech: The US allocated about $440m (£358m) in assistance to South Africa in 2023, according to US government data.

a2042.speaker: South African government
a2042.speech: Says that the new law does not allow arbitrary seizures of land as it must first attempt to reach an agreement with the owner, and says that the current system of "willing seller, willing buyer" has allowed white farmers to delay the process of land reform.

a2042.speaker: Vincent Magwenya, spokesperson for the South African president
a2042.speech: Said last month that the state "may not expropriate property arbitrarily or for a purpose other than… in the public interest".

a2042.speaker: South African government spokesperson (2018, anonymous)
a2042.speech: South Africa then accused Trump of seeking to sow division, with a spokesperson saying he was "misinformed".

a2115.speaker: Dr Ahmed Robleh Abdilleh, Minister of Health of Djibouti
a2115.speech: In his address, recalled that the fight against malaria was everyone's business, specifying that in Djibouti the incidence of the disease had been falling since 2021, from 73.5 cases per 1,000 inhabitants in 2020 to 38 cases per 1,000 in 2023 ; reaffirmed his Ministry's commitment to work to stimulate investment in the fight against malaria, particularly in the development of new tools, in order to propel the country onto the path leading to the elimination of the disease ; came back to the high-impact actions, namely vector control with the destruction of larval breeding sites, indoor residual spraying and space and aerial spraying ; and finally asked all stakeholders to continue raising the population's awareness in order to trigger real change.

a2115.speaker: Farahad Hassan Farah, Representative of the World Health Organization (WHO) in Djibouti
a2115.speech: Reiterated the WHO's commitment to accompany the Ministry of Health in achieving the objectives of malaria elimination in Djibouti.

a2592.speaker: UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and World Health Organization (WHO)
a2592.speech: Express deep concern at the escalating forced displacement crisis, the deterioration of health care infrastructure and widespread humanitarian challenges in Sudan.

a2592.speaker: Margaret Harris, WHO spokesperson
a2592.speech: Said the prolonged conflict in Sudan has pushed the health system to its limits, with massive displacement, epidemics, war wounded, non-communicable diseases and maternal and child health needs increasing in the face of a decreasing capacity to meet these demands.

a2592.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) records
a2592.speech: Has recorded, since 15 April, 60 attacks against health facilities, resulting in 34 deaths and 38 injuries; and reported cholera outbreaks amounting to 6,939 cases and 200 deaths in nine states.

a2592.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) latest projection update
a2592.speech: Reveals that acute food insecurity will affect 17.7 million people between October 2023 and February 2024, with about 4.9 million people in IPC phase 4 (Emergency) and nearly 12.8 million in IPC phase 3 (Crisis).

a2592.speaker: Humanitarian agencies (estimates)
a2592.speech: Estimate that 24.7 million people are in need of assistance; the revised Humanitarian Response Plan launched in May 2023 targets 18.1 million people.

a2592.speaker: General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Sudanese army chief
a2592.speech: Accused the head of the United Nations mission, Volker Perthes, of stoking the conflict.

a2592.speaker: Sudanese authorities / Sudanese military government
a2592.speech: Had for several months voiced criticism of the effectiveness of the United Nations Integrated Transition Assistance Mission in Sudan (UNITAMS), declared Volker Perthes “persona non grata”, and made known their wish to put an end to UN operations.

a2592.speaker: UN Security Council
a2592.speech: Confirmed the termination of the Mission on 1 December.

a2700.speaker: Sir Isaac Newton
a2700.speech: Once wrote: "If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants."

a2700.speaker: Glenn Maguire, Chief Economist for South Asia, ASEAN & Pacific
a2700.speech: Once reflected on Singapore's development miracle. He noted that few economic transformations have been as rapid, enduring and successful. Singapore's rise was born of necessity after its expulsion from Malaysia in 1965; Lee's policy choices and pragmatism were inseparable from the country's success.

a2700.speaker: Lee Kuan Yew, founding Prime Minister of Singapore
a2700.speech: Emphasised excellence in public service and recruited the best minds to drive the country's progress; he believed in paying ministers well to ensure integrity and accountability in government.

a2700.speaker: Dr Albert Winsemius, economist dispatched by the United Nations (feasibility study)
a2700.speech: His recommendations led to a 10-year development plan focused on turning Singapore into a manufacturing hub.

a2742.speaker: Mohamed Aden Guelleh, MENFOP regional inspector of Ali-Sabieh
a2742.speech: Welcomed all the participants and stressed that this gathering of the various partners of public school education aims to raise awareness and discuss with parents the importance and positive contributions of preschool education. He explained that there are now twenty-nine preschool classes in Ali Sabieh and in all rural localities, thanks to the considerable efforts of the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training.

a2742.speaker: Charmake Hassan Allaleh, President of the regional council
a2742.speech: Expressed his joy at taking part in fruitful discussions on the future of the region's children. He paid solemn tribute to parents, teachers and school heads for their ongoing commitment to the school education of the country's children. He assured that the regional authorities are available to take part in building the future of our schoolchildren.

a2742.speaker: Loula Ali Elabe, Director of Public Education, MENFOP
a2742.speech: Recalled that the objective of this noble project of the United States Agency for International Development, USAID, involving the Ministry of Women and Family and the National Union of Djiboutian Women (UNFD), is to support and encourage communities to integrate play as an essential component in children's learning and development, to equip and to advocate for preschool education. She added that MENFOP is working to expand preschool by 2030, recalling the establishment of the first schools in the most disadvantaged areas to give a chance to the most deprived.

a2742.speaker: Romain Babagbeto, head of the USAID “Play to Learn” project
a2742.speech: Said that this campaign marks a decisive stage in the implementation of the project: “It gives us the opportunity to go and meet communities through educational talks in order to generate the involvement and commitment of parents.”

a2742.speaker: Abdillahi Omar Ibrahim, interim programme coordinator of the National Union of Djiboutian Women (UNFD)
a2742.speech: Explained, on the subject of community engagement, that it is essential that individually and collectively — parents, teachers, policymakers, civil society and the community in general — mobilise so that these changes take place everywhere in all the regions of the country, referring to the popular saying: “It takes a whole village to educate a child.” He recalled the importance of the commitment of parents, and especially of the mother, in the child's development during this crucial period of life.

a2742.speaker: Saïda Waberi Assoweh, Deputy Prefect of Ali-Sabieh
a2742.speech: Announced that the “Play to Learn” theme of the USAID project is very interesting for the school future of our children, and that the best way for schoolchildren to learn is one that presents lessons in a playful way.

a2813.speaker: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) (press release of 20 September 2013)
a2813.speech: expressed concern about the situation in the Central African Republic and its humanitarian consequences for the population, victims of recent hostilities in the north-west, more precisely in Bossangoa and Bouca; according to the ICRC, the entire population is currently in the bush.

a2813.speaker: Stefan Bigler, head of an ICRC team that travelled to the town of Bouca
a2813.speech: "Civilians are the first victims of the violence. The priority is to treat the wounded and to assist families whose homes have been burned or looted. The dead, who are sometimes left lying abandoned, must also be buried." ; "People fled, leaving everything behind. They took refuge in the bush, with relatives, or in religious compounds," he added, before specifying that the ICRC had airlifted 13 seriously wounded people from Batangafo to the referral hospital in Bangui, and that within the space of a week 30 bodies had been taken in hand by volunteers of the Central African Red Cross in order to identify and bury them.

a2813.speaker: Bonaventure Bazirutwabo, ICRC health coordinator
a2813.speech: "Far from the capital, access to care is extremely difficult and the needs are immense!"

a2813.speaker: Georgios Georgantas, head of the ICRC delegation in Bangui
a2813.speech: "All those involved must refrain from any act of violence against civilians as well as against medical personnel and facilities." ; "It is essential that the security of humanitarian organisations be ensured so that we can have access to all the victims and provide them with assistance. It is a matter of survival for the population."

a2936.speaker: Milingo Lungu, former KCM provisional liquidator
a2936.speech: Had filed an application for an order staying proceedings pending determination of his appeal against the Economic and Financial Crimes Court's ruling dated August 3, 2023, in which it held that it had jurisdiction to determine the matter ; contended that the same court did not have jurisdiction to determine the DPP's application on the basis of the cases that are pending determination in other courts ; argued that his appeal would be rendered an academic exercise if the Court of Appeal pronounced that the Economic and Financial Crimes Court was not properly constituted.

a2936.speaker: Judges Pixie Yangailo, Ann Malata-Ononuju and Mwanajiti Mabbolobbolo, Economic and Financial Crimes Court (ruling)
a2936.speech: Said the appeal would not succeed and only served to protract the judicial proceedings before court. "Furthermore, we have combed through the affidavits, skeleton arguments and submissions and have found no exceptional circumstances or ambit of the requirements set out in the plethora of authorities for grant of stay of proceedings pending appeal," said the court.

a2936.speaker: Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP)
a2936.speech: Seeks an order for the three accounts alleged with tainted property, to be forfeited to the State, pursuant to Section 29 and 31 of the forfeiture of proceeds of Crime.

a2936.speaker: Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) investigations
a2936.speech: According to DEC investigations, it is alleged that Mr Lungu took advantage of his position as KCM liquidator and stole $40 million belonging to the mining firm. The said accounts were opened in 2021.

a2936.speaker: Milingo Lungu, former KCM provisional liquidator
a2936.speech: Has however declined any illegal dealings in respect of the funds. He stated that he is a preferential creditor and has a bona fide claim of right to transfer the funds for payment or security pursuant to his right of remuneration.

a3051.speaker: United Nations
a3051.speech: said on Thursday that global aid funding cuts, led by the United States, are disrupting efforts to vaccinate children against deadly diseases almost as much as the COVID-19 pandemic did.

a3051.speaker: World Health Organization offices in 108 largely low and lower-middle income countries (reports)
a3051.speech: Emergency and routine vaccinations were significantly affected in nearly half of countries at the start of April due to the funding cuts, according to reports from World Health Organization offices in 108 largely low and lower-middle income countries.

a3051.speaker: WHO and UNICEF, in a joint release with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
a3051.speech: said cuts to funding also reduced vaccine supplies and hampered disease surveillance ; said COVID-19 caused what was called the largest backslide in childhood vaccination in a generation, and aid funding cuts, led by the U.S. - formerly the world's largest donor - risked the same outcome ; called for funding for childhood immunisation to be maintained ahead of Gavi's funding round, which will be launched in June, with the group seeking $9 billion for its work from 2026-2030 ; said measles cases have increased year-on-year since 2021, while meningitis surged in Africa last year and yellow fever cases also rose after declines in the last decade.

a3051.speaker: Catherine Russell, UNICEF executive director
a3051.speech: "Setbacks (are) at a similar level to what we saw during COVID-19. We cannot afford to lose ground in the fight against preventable disease."

a3051.speaker: Sania Nishtar, Gavi's chief executive officer
a3051.speech: said it was possible to fight the rise of infectious diseases but only if the group is fully funded.

a3051.speaker: Internal U.S. government document
a3051.speech: Last month, an internal U.S. government document showed it would follow its cuts to UNICEF and the WHO, part of wider plans to streamline and focus foreign aid to align with the "America First" policy, by cancelling its contribution of around $300 million annually to Gavi.

a3051.speaker: U.S. State Department
a3051.speech: told Reuters last week it had nominated Mark Lloyd, assistant administrator for global health, to Gavi's 28-person board.

a3051.speaker: U.S. State Department and Gavi
a3051.speech: Both the U.S. State Department and Gavi declined to comment about what this could mean for U.S. funding.

a3140.speaker: Peter Shivute, Chief Justice of Namibia
a3140.speech: said Smuts authored over 130 reported judgments at the High Court and more than 80 at the Supreme Court ; “As you retire, you leave behind a legacy of intellectual rigour, fairness and commitment to justice. May your retirement be both restful and rewarding” ; “These accomplishments underscore not only his intellect but also his relentless pursuit of excellence.”

a3144.speaker: Human Rights Defenders Coalition
a3144.speech: termed the demand of Malawians who took to the streets for months as “electoral justice”.

a3144.speaker: Akim Mwale, Lilongwe city resident and registered voter
a3144.speech: says the country cannot afford another mess the size of the mass protests that disrupted livelihoods and business for almost a year ; “As we count down to the 2025 General Elections, the Malawi Electoral Commision and all stakeholders should see to it that we do the right things to avoid the costly but preventable blunders we witnessed in 2019. We don’t want to waste time protesting against a badly managed election, but doing things that will uplift our lives, families and country. The road to credible elections begins now. What we do today will define how the citizenry welcome the outcome” ; urges the electoral management body to be attentive and responsive to citizen concerns throughout the electoral process, including voter registration.

a3144.speaker: Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC)
a3144.speech: reports that it has registered over seven million voters despite low turnout and concerns that gaps in the issuance of the citizens’ identity cards—the sole legally accepted proof for voter identification—would exclude some eligible voters.

a3144.speaker: Bishop Gilford Matonga, Chisankho Watch board chairperson
a3144.speech: says the coalition’s primary purpose is to observe elections to enhance transparency, inclusivity and credibility throughout the electoral process; touts the observatory to become an inclusive and evidence-based coalition that fosters innovative and sustainable election observation practices in the country ; “This coalition is important because it will help ensure that the coming elections are credible, free, fair and that Malawians should be satisfied. We, therefore, encourage Malawians to never give up but participate in the electoral process and trust that there are independent institutions like Chisankho Watch working tirelessly throughout the electoral process to ensure that the people’s will is respected” ; continued that the organisations determined to keep an eye on the next poll are trustworthy, with a long-standing history in elections observation, and said Chisankho Watch affiliates have evidence-based reputation in data collection, which he said assures Malawians of the reliability of the coalition’s observations.

a3144.speaker: Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace (CCJP)
a3144.speech: promises that the coalition will promote meaningful citizen participation by engaging diverse stakeholders, including marginalised groups in elections observation and civic education.

a3144.speaker: Boniface Chibwana, CCJP national coordinator and head of the Centre of Multiparty Democracy
a3144.speech: “Among others, Chisankho Watch will conduct observation of the fresh voter registration process which is about to begin, hold advocacy engagements with key stakeholders like MEC, process and verify results of the 2025 elections for transparency, and observe the pre-and post-elections environment in Malawi. The coalition envisages credible, inclusive and transparent elections for a peaceful and democratic Malawi.”

a3144.speaker: Dr Henry Chingaipe, electoral governance expert
a3144.speech: said in his keynote address during the launch that local electoral observers strengthens election transparency, mitigates electoral manipulation and identifies legal gaps and deviations from the law; said domestic observation mission help determine the legitimacy of the government that comes out from the electoral process.

a3144.speaker: Dr Sarah Limbikani Kamlongera, MEC commissioner
a3144.speech: said the coalition will enhance collaboration between the election management body and the organisations that are party to national efforts to deliver a transparent and credible election in 2025 ; “The coalition allows for partnership and collaboration that will ease communication on electoral issues and which help MEC to develop more confidence in the entire process knowing that every stakeholder out there is watching and is interested in the electoral process.”

a3186.speaker: National Communications Authority (NCA) Somalia and Somali Bureau of Standards (joint public notice)
a3186.speech: The notice, in line with Article 59 of the Communications Law, emphasizes the importance of complying with these regulations to ensure a fair and competitive market and the protection of consumers and licensees ; The notice also shows that any existing telecom equipment currently in use, which has yet to be certified by the NCA, must be submitted for certification promptly, and that failure to comply with this process violates the law and may significantly disrupt the overall telecom infrastructure ; The notice concludes by emphasizing that the NCA cannot be held liable for any damages from using illegal or unauthorized equipment, including new technologies such as 5G, and that it is the operator's responsibility to adhere to the approved standards and guidelines.

a3186.speaker: Mustafa Yassin Sheikh, General Manager of the NCA (National Communications Authority of Somalia)
a3186.speech: "All telecom equipment, regardless of its origin, must undergo the necessary approval process jointly conducted by the NCA and SOBS. This 'Type Approval' process guarantees that the equipment meets the required standards and poses no potential medical risks or interference to other licensees." ; "It is important to understand that any communications equipment invested in by operators without obtaining proper approval from the NCA will be considered illegal. The NCA will take necessary actions to ensure compliance, which may include imposing penalties, fines, or even revoking licenses, as deemed appropriate."

a3186.speaker: National Communications Authority (NCA) Somalia
a3186.speech: The NCA encourages all licensed operators to review their existing inventory of telecom equipment and initiate the necessary steps to ensure compliance with the regulatory requirements.

a3202.speaker: Study by researchers from the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (UTHealth) and Baylor College of Medicine, published in the American Journal of Physiology-Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology
a3202.speech: Found differences between the lung physiology and immune function of children and adults, shedding light on why children are more resilient against Covid-19.

a3202.speaker: The researchers (in their paper)
a3202.speech: Note that in the first 149 082 positive Covid-19 cases in the US, a low 1.7% of cases were infants, children and adolescents under the age of 18.

a3202.speaker: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
a3202.speech: Three paediatric deaths were identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of April 2020.

a3202.speaker: Matthew Harting, assistant professor in the Department of Pediatric Surgery at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth and senior author of the paper
a3202.speech: “ACE2 are important for viral entry and there seems to be less of them in children, because they increase with age.”

a3202.speaker: The researchers
a3202.speech: Explained that children's immune systems respond differently to viruses than those of adults, which leaves a smaller chance for severe illness in paediatric patients, through various mechanisms such as the retention of T-cells in children, which have the ability to fight off or limit inflammation.

a3202.speaker: Harry Karmouty-Quintana, assistant professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at McGovern Medical School and co-author of the paper
a3202.speech: “In severe cases of adult Covid-19 patients, we've seen that those T-cells are reduced, so the ability to fight the virus is also reduced. In kids, those T-cells seem to be maintained, so they are still able to prevent the virus” ; Commented that patients with higher levels of T-cells have higher levels of Interleukin 10 (IL-10), an anti-inflammatory cytokine, and that children also have a higher concentration of regulator T-cells in their lung tissue ; “IL-10 inhibits the inflammation of other components like IL-6 that are detrimental. Adults tend to experience hyperinflammatory states, where kids do not. In preclinical studies in mice, IL-10 has also shown to decrease with age.”

a3202.speaker: Matthew Harting, assistant professor in the Department of Pediatric Surgery at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth and senior author of the paper
a3202.speech: Stressed the importance of collaborations such as this study because they can shed critical insight into why the disease behaves differently in children compared to older people: “Even now, as we're learning about effective treatments, we're seeing younger people handle this disease better than older people. Moving forward, physicians and scientists need multidisciplinary collaboration to continue learning. This is just another step in the right direction to attack this virus.”

a3556.speaker: Human Rights Watch (rights group)
a3556.speech: Said at least 120 children have been abducted in Mozambique and that there had been a resurgence of attacks and child kidnappings in the last two months, and called on Mozambique’s government to do more to find the children and prevent further abductions.

a3556.speaker: Witnesses (unnamed)
a3556.speech: Have said that children abducted from towns and villages have been used as fighters in subsequent attacks.

a3556.speaker: United Nations
a3556.speech: Said the violence has displaced more than 600,000 people and spilled into neighbouring provinces.

a3556.speaker: Jan Egeland, Secretary General of the Norwegian Refugee Council
