a7072.speech: According to the consultations, for decades Eswatini has grappled with a key impediment to its growth, the slow progress towards higher-value production; the consultations underscored that this challenge has persisted far too long, and the time for change is now, and revealed clear agreement on the need to focus on two strategic priority areas: investing in climate-resilient infrastructure and strengthening competitiveness.

a7072.speaker: CSP mission team
a7072.speech: Proposed an aggressive strategy to tackle this economic bottleneck, accelerating structural transformation.

a7072.speaker: Country Strategy Paper (CSP) 2025-2030 report
a7072.speech: "Stakeholders overwhelmingly endorsed this approach, recognizing that the key to long-term prosperity lies in moving away from outdated systems and embracing a more diversified and innovative economic model." ; "The coming years will be crucial in shaping Eswatini's economic future. With the right investments, collaboration, and commitment, the Kingdom has the chance to turn its economic challenges into opportunities for sustainable growth, inclusive development."

a7072.speaker: Stakeholders (government ministries, private sector leaders and development partners)
a7072.speech: Agreed that boosting private sector development, from entrepreneurship to large-scale industry, must be a priority; there was a strong consensus that achieving these goals requires enhanced coordination between the government, development partners, and the private sector.

a7072.speaker: Government of Eswatini
a7072.speech: Has expressed strong support for the CSP and commended the work of the Bank in facilitating successful consultations; the government recognized the milestone achievements in driving the country's socio-economic development and highlighted the importance of continued collaboration between stakeholders ; sees the establishment of the Liaison Office as essential for strengthening the relationship between Eswatini and international partners, and called for a bolstered presence at this office to ensure smoother communication and more impactful outcomes as Eswatini's portfolio grows.

a7186.speaker: Judith-Ann Walker, executive director of the development Research and Projects Centre (dRPC)
a7186.speech: Over N150 million was granted to local Nigerian nonprofits working in local communities, changing the lives of thousands of vulnerable groups, women, and children under the NSI project, according to Judith-Ann Walker, who stressed during the launch that the programme is a strategic investment in local resilience rather than just a band-aid solution. “Local organisations are frequently the ones who suffer the most when development partners withdraw or stop funding,” Ms Walker stated. “In addition to providing short-term assistance, this programme equips our partners with the resources, guidance, and strategic ability necessary to attract new donors and become self-sufficient.”

a7186.speaker: Judith-Ann Walker, executive director of dRPC
a7186.speech: “We see this as a bridge, not just between past and future finance, but between dependency and self-reliance. We hope that these NGOs will go on to implement projects and even provide funding to others in the future.”

a7186.speaker: Stanley Ukpai, director of projects at dRPC
a7186.speech: “Donors like to collaborate with local partners who are open, responsible, and technically proficient,” stated Stanley Ukpai. “We want to make sure that no promising NGO is overlooked because they are unable to interact with or maintain international partners.”

a7186.speaker: Grace Ibrahim, executive director of a women-led NGO in Borno State
a7186.speech: According to Grace Ibrahim, the mentorship has improved her organisation's accountability procedures and proposal-writing approach. “We thought it was finished when our USAID funding stopped,” she added. “We were able to restore our confidence and processes thanks to the dRPC coaching. We are now preparing our first independent proposal and negotiating with two new contributors.”

a7186.speaker: development Research and Projects Centre (dRPC)
a7186.speech: is extending an open invitation to international donors, foundations, and development agencies to collaborate in scaling up the model, to ensure that local NGOs remain sustainable, open, and significant players in Nigeria's development landscape.

a7311.speaker: Rev. Brian Kamwendo, Presidential Adviser on Religious Affairs
a7311.speech: Standing by his claim that 5,300 clerics have benefitted from K8.3 billion in loans; speaking in an interview last evening, he shrugged off the growing skepticism from Malawi's top religious institutions, saying the loans were deliberately targeted at "fraternal clerics" under a pilot phase of the Faith Leaders Empowerment Scheme, not through official church channels: "We started with the fraternal because this was just a pilot phase with an expectation that we will later engage the mother bodies. So, it is not strange that they don't know who have benefitted."

a7311.speaker: National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF)
a7311.speech: Is standing by the claim that 5,300 clerics have benefitted from K8.3 billion in loans, despite major religious umbrella bodies distancing themselves from the scheme.

a7311.speaker: Whyghtone Mweta, NEEF credit manager
a7311.speech: Clarified that the clerics accessed the funds after forming groups, and were engaged in various businesses like grocery shops, farming, and mobile money services: "They are part of the broader ecosystem of Malawian entrepreneurs. We treat them as any eligible Malawian who can benefit from Neef loans."

a7311.speaker: Malawi Conference of Catholic Bishops (MCCB), Malawi Council of Churches (MCC) and Muslim Association of Malawi (MAM)
a7311.speech: Have all publicly distanced themselves from Kamwendo's announcement made during the July 5 national worship service marking Malawi's 61st independence anniversary.

a7311.speaker: Fr. Valeriano Mtseka, MCCB general secretary
a7311.speech: Said he was unaware of any Catholic cleric - bishop or priest - who had benefitted from the loans.

a7311.speaker: Rev. Billy Gama, MCC board chairperson
a7311.speech: "Actually, I was right there at the prayers and I was shocked when I heard that statement. To the best of my knowledge, no one [from MCC] has benefitted. It might have been a political statement."

a7311.speaker: Sheikh Dinala Chabulika, MAM spokesperson
a7311.speech: Said his association moved quickly to verify Kamwendo's claims - only to find "zero" beneficiaries among its members: "Write [the story] and tell them [government] that we [MAM] haven't found anyone [who received Neef loans]."

a7311.speaker: Report alleging K5.8 billion was disbursed to 11 pastors
a7311.speech: A separate report alleged that K5.8 billion was disbursed to just 11 pastors under a purported presidential initiative.

a7311.speaker: National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF)
a7311.speech: Refuted a separate report alleging that K5.8 billion was disbursed to just 11 pastors under a purported presidential initiative.

a7311.speaker: National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF)
a7311.speech: Said earlier this year it aimed to disburse K150 billion to over 400,000 farmers and entrepreneurs by March 2025; by January this year, the fund had already disbursed K184 billion, reaching over 200,000 Malawians.

a7411.speaker: Tesfaye Beljige (PhD), the ruling party's whip
a7411.speech: “For 50 years, only the government offered agricultural extension services. Now the bill seeks to open this role to the private sector,” told lawmakers ; said his administration plans to reduce problems of access, quality and poor service and to build “a digital, standardised, efficient, accessible and accountable” system that will “boost agricultural-centre efficiency.”

a7411.speaker: Draft proclamation/bill tabled in Parliament on May 27, 2025 (text)
a7411.speech: The seven-section, 40-article bill says any provider seeking a license should register with the authorities and supply “not less than three” kinds of agricultural inputs and extension services ; mandates that the Ministry of Agriculture and regional bureaus launch short-, medium-, and long-term agricultural initiatives independently, in partnership with approved providers, or through project-based arrangements.

a7411.speaker: Azmeraw Andom (MP)
a7411.speech: Warned that a clause allowing non-government providers to set their payment terms “could undermine the proclamation’s purpose” and urged that it be amended before final approval.

a7411.speaker: Almaw Tigabu (MP)
a7411.speech: Said many farmers were frustrated with the existing extension workers: “We used to receive multiple services from a single expert. But now, despite the increase in the number of experts, those services are no longer available. Even when farmers are interested in improved extension services, they often cannot access them.” ; argued that “knowledgeable farmers should be enabled to provide extension services to others” and emphasised “the need for a regulatory body to oversee all service providers, monitor service quality and ensure accountability through proper assessment mechanisms.”

a7411.speaker: Zemene Ferede, farmer in Armacho Woreda, West Gondar Zone, Amhara Regional State
a7411.speech: Sees extension officers often prioritise large landowners and investors over smallholders: “We get the service only by pleading,” he told Fortune ; hopes private competition will make the system accessible, but fears that if private providers charge too much, smallholder farmers may struggle to access these services.

a7411.speaker: Atnafu Fanta, grower near Arbaminch, South Ethiopia Regional State
a7411.speech: Echoed that worry, criticised the services currently offered and said private extension agents “should consider the needs of low-income farmers above all.”

a7411.speaker: Desalegn Ayansa, market-research specialist for the Liben Farmers’ Cooperative Union in Woliso
a7411.speech: Quibbled that many extension workers are trained in a particular discipline and have a limited skill set to address the diverse queries of farmers: “Farmers want to know about not only farming but also animals and the environment. But, these experts can only advise on one topic,” he told Fortune ; believes private providers, driven by profit motives, would offer better support, yet fears that because farmers are accustomed to free services, they might resist paying.

a7411.speaker: Serku Tarekegh, manager of the Ras Gaynt Farmers’ Cooperative Union
a7411.speech: Supports private involvement but doubts that companies will be able to satisfy demand.

a7411.speaker: Beriso Feyisa, deputy head of the Oromia Agriculture Bureau
a7411.speech: Said talk of inflated fees comes from “misreading the draft,” stating that private operators are required to work “within the government framework” ; “The measure is designed to benefit farmers and address existing limitations in the agricultural sector,” he told Fortune.

a7411.speaker: Tesfakidan Admasu, head of Agriculture & Development at St. Mary’s University
a7411.speech: Called the move “long overdue”: “Poor access and quality in government services make private involvement potentially beneficial for farmers” ; criticised the bill for not spelling out what the extension services should entail in each sector and how artificial intelligence (AI) can support these efforts, and urged lawmakers to clarify service scopes, establish a non-governmental body to evaluate the quality and impact of private services, and outline clear fee guidelines.

a7438.speaker: Joseph Nyumah Boakai, President of Liberia
a7438.speech: Has emphasized the urgent need to attract foreign direct investment (FDI) to generate large-scale employment opportunities for Liberian youth; acknowledged that local businesses alone cannot absorb the growing number of unemployed young people in the country; said that bridging the unemployment gap requires strategic concessions and investments that will unlock sustainable job opportunities across the country.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: Reiterated the president's commitment to job creation but noted that maintaining those jobs is a shared responsibility. "While the government will do its part to create jobs, the people must also do their part in protecting them," he stated; said the recent incidents of violence, particularly at mining companies, which resulted in the burning of some company facilities, were deeply concerning; stated that due to the destruction, hospitals and schools owned by those companies were forced to shut down, leading to significant job losses; emphasized that while the government is working to create employment opportunities, citizens must equally work to protect and sustain those jobs.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: Noted that the cabinet meeting's reform efforts in critical government sectors - rule of law, security, education, healthcare, infrastructure development, donor funding, and road rehabilitation - aim to strengthen governance and drive national development.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: Revealed that one major area of concern highlighted during the meeting was airport security; said the president has prioritized strengthening security at the airport to curb mineral trafficking; warned that Liberia's international airport could face sanctions if it does not maintain global safety standards.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: Said the President at the meeting also called for full transparency in ongoing investigations into corruption and mismanagement cases and urged that they be concluded swiftly.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: Disclosed that the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) has reduced funding to Liberia, impacting critical sectors such as education and healthcare; said the USAID cut has particularly affected the HIV/AIDS program, which provides essential medication for people living with the disease. "The drugs are not meant to be paid for, but the AIDS Commission is now struggling due to low budgetary support after the USAID cut," Piah explained. He noted that the commission has engaged the president on the issue, emphasizing the need to find solutions that will prevent the funding shortfall from worsening conditions for those affected; noted that despite the cut Liberia continues to receive significant aid, with the country's overall donor portfolio standing at approximately $500 million, of which USAID contributed around $87 million; reassured the public that the government is exploring alternative funding sources to offset the shortfall.

a7438.speaker: Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA)
a7438.speech: Informed the president that efforts to increase domestic revenue collection could help mitigate the impact of reduced donor funding.

a7438.speaker: Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberian Information Minister
a7438.speech: "If the LRA meets its target and increases the national budget to $1.2 billion, it could help cover the gap left by the USAID suspension," he added.

a7515.speaker: Analysts
a7515.speech: Observe that Kabambe's unexpected landslide victory in UTM Party's elective convention — against heavyweights, Patricia Kaliati, Newton Kambala and Matthews Mtumbuka — has unsettled some confidence in presidential aspirants and Mwaungulu is one of them.

a7515.speaker: Dunstain Mwaungulu, former Supreme Court judge and presidential aspirant (Facebook post)
a7515.speech: Touts himself as the "best President for the Malawi economy, economists and economics": "I am challenging Dr Kabambe on his policies — and record! I think l am the best custodian of the Malawi economy than Dr.Kabambe. He was in the Ministry of Finance (in charge of budgets) for a spell and that means that the difficulties this economy has had in the past and during his tenure are partly caused or exacerbated by him. And then he was Governor of the Reserve Bank — at the centre of monetary policy. What has he got to show for this? I checked his vision in a recent write-up — it is just a pipedream because it does not show what has to be done in the economy to realise the vision and visions. I will hammer this in my campaign and debate him. I am running simply because of the economy and l think that l have better approaches to solving the economic riddle of Malawi."

a7515.speaker: Anonymous source (Maravi Express source)
